newsitem.title: USA: U.S. anti-drug troops pulled from Mexico border.
newsitem.headline: U.S. anti-drug troops pulled from Mexico border.

text.p: U.S. ground troops have halted anti-drug foot patrols of the Mexican border as part of the fallout from a marine shooting of an 18-year-old shepherd in May, the Pentagon said on Tuesday.

The 200 or so soldiers and marines "walking point" to support the overall U.S. anti-drug effort have been been withdrawn pending the outcome of a review of their mission, Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said.
He said a chief focus of the review was whether the troops were adequately protected from civil or criminal liability for their actions while carrying out their jobs.
The retreat involved a relatively small part of the effort mounted by the United States to thwart drug-smuggling from Mexico, a major transshipment point for marijuana and cocaine.

"Right now there are a small number of people who would have been patrolling the border (who) are not patrolling the border," Bacon told reporters. He noted that neither the much larger Border Patrol, a law enforcement agency, nor military surveillance and other intelligence-gathering were affected.
"So the border is not unguarded. It's not unpatrolled. That work continues," he said.

Defence Secretary William Cohen issued the order halting the missions on Thursday without an announcement in an effort to play down its significance, Army Col. Dick Bridges, a Pentagon spokesman, said.

He said the Pentagon wanted to avoid the appearance of interfering in court proceedings in the shooting case. A grand jury is considering whether to indict one or more of the marines involved in the shooting in Redford, a Texas town southeast of El Paso where the 18-year-old was killed.

Bacon left open the possibility that the Pentagon review might conclude it was inappropriate for U.S. military forces to be involved in Border Patrol activities along the 2,000-mile (3,218 kilometre) frontier.

He said that the military remained very committed to supporting the U.S. war on drugs. He estimated that the Defence Department was spending as much as $800 million to $1 billion a year to support the effort.
Along the border itself, the Pentagon estimates that every dollar it spends on supporting the anti-drug effort yields about $50 in seizures of illegal drugs.
"So we think we're playing an important role. We will continue to play a role of some sort. The question is what that role will be," Bacon said.
Pentagon officials said the policy review was considering possible new rules for military interaction with both civilians and civilian law enforcement personnel.

In this case, the Defence Department would submit proposed revised procedures to the authorities of the Southwestern states where troops had been involved in anti-drug efforts -- Texas, Arizona, New Mexico and California, Bridges said.

In New Mexico, U.S. border agents proposed putting up a huge concrete barrier in the small town of Columbus to halt a sharp rise in illegal immigration and drug trafficking, officials said on Tuesday.
Columbus, a town of just 800 people, has become a popular crossing point for illegal immigrants and drug smugglers.
